name: Playing Not Spraying
beta: Opens with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system with finger cracks, crosses right below a roof into a splitter crack to a mid-route ledge, then a second roof leads to a hand crack and stemming corners with a hard exit, topping out via a deep summit chimney; protection is cams and nuts to 3 inches throughout.
overview: Playing Not Spraying (5.10, Grade III, 8 pitches, 800 ft) climbs the clean white granite south face of Silver Horn, a rarely-climbed sub-summit of Silver Star Mountain at Washington Pass.

current.approach: The Silver Horn is a sub-summit on the east ridge of Silver Star Mountain, east of the main summit, and both of its routes are on the clean white granite of its south face. That face is not reached from the Wine Spires pullout or Burgundy Col, which serve the other side of the crest. Instead, walk the Cedar Creek Trail from its trailhead at the end of FR 5310-200, off SR-20 about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turnoff. After roughly five miles, turn off to the right below the old burn and follow a rough path up the right-hand side of the creek that drains the south side of the Silver Horn. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping below the face.
approach_variant_names: Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side
current.descent: Descend by making a series of rappels down the SE side of Silver Horn. A 70-meter rope is recommended, and carrying extra/bulk webbing is advisable since fixed rappel anchors are sparse and some anchors must be built from scratch.
current.detailed_rack: Cams and nuts to 3 inches
rack: Standard alpine rack to 3in, doubles in common mid sizes
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack; cams and nuts up to 3" cover the route
bivy: Meadows below the Silver Horn's south face
current.rope_note: A 70 m rope. The descent is a series of rappels down the southeast side of Silver Horn, fixed anchors there are sparse, and some have to be built from scratch - so carry extra bulk webbing and cord for them on top of the rack. Cams and nuts to 3 inches cover the eight pitches, which open with a layback off a clean flake into corner and finger-crack systems and finish up a deep summit chimney. Protect that chimney well before mantling out onto the top.

name: Pinnacle Saddle / North Slopes
beta: This is the standard and essentially only documented way up Plummer Peak. Hike the maintained Pinnacle Peak Trail from Reflection Lakes through forest and talus to the saddle between Pinnacle and Plummer Peaks (~5,950 ft). At the saddle, leave the maintained tread and follow a well-worn boot path that curves right/west and then climbs the north side/ridge of Plummer, passing a seasonal tarn, to top out on the small (50x15 ft) summit block. The final ~400 ft above the saddle is loose, sometimes steep Class 2 terrain with a couple of short hands-on steps; a few well-placed trees aid the last moves. No rope or protection is used on this route.
overview: Plummer Peak (6,374 ft) is the seventh-highest summit in the Tatoosh Range, a compact ridge of eroded Miocene granodiorite (the Tatoosh pluton) overlain by older Fifes Peak/Stevens Ridge volcanics, rising directly south of Paradise in Mount Rainier National Park. It's reached via the Pinnacle Peak Trail from Reflection Lakes, sharing the first 1.3 miles with the route to Pinnacle Peak before an easy scramble breaks off west to the summit. A small tarn sits just below the top, and the summit gives one of the closest, most complete views of Mount Rainier in the park, along with views south to Mount Adams, Mount St. Helens, and the Goat Rocks. The peak was named for Fred G. Plummer, a U.S. Forest Service cartographer and Tacoma geography teacher.

current.approach: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road (1.4 miles east of the Paradise-Longmire Road junction, roughly 1.9 miles from the Paradise turnoff). The signed Pinnacle Peak Trail (no official trail number; it's a Mount Rainier NP maintained trail) leaves from the south side of the road, directly across from the largest of the Reflection Lakes (approx. 46.7683, -121.7314). The trail climbs moderately through mountain hemlock and Alaska yellow cedar forest for the first half-mile; around 0.5 mi you get a first partial view of Rainier through the trees, and at about 0.6 mi you cross a seasonal stream/cascading creek that is the only reliable water on the hike (dry by late summer in low-snow years). By 0.7 mi the trail breaks out of forest into open talus and heather slopes below the cliffs of Pinnacle Peak, and steepens noticeably from here — this is where lingering snow (well into July on the shaded, north-facing switchbacks) creates the trail's main hazard, since a slip on hard morning snow above the talus can slide a hiker into rock. Around 0.9-1.0 mi the trail passes beneath the impressive cliff bands on Pinnacle's north face, then switchbacks up a short, exposed final pitch (the trail's best viewpoint) to reach Pinnacle/Pinnacle Saddle (Pinnacle Gap) at about 1.25-1.3 mi and roughly 5,920-5,960 ft. This saddle is the trail's official end and the crux junction: unmaintained user paths fork east toward Pinnacle Peak/The Castle and west toward Plummer and Denman peaks. For Plummer Peak, continue a short distance past the saddle and look for a climbers' path branching right (west); it crosses a flat rocky shelf holding a seasonal tarn, where a fork continues straight toward Denman — instead bear left (south/uphill) onto the boot path that climbs the open, rocky north-facing slopes of Plummer Peak. This upper section is unmaintained, loose in spots, and route-finding is straightforward but the tread is thin; a short class 2-3 scramble (brief hands-on-rock moves, some loose blocks, mild exposure) gains the last few hundred feet to the 6,374 ft summit. A lingering snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July — either kick steps straight up it or skirt left on the rockier tread; both options rejoin near the top.
approach_variant_names: Pinnacle Saddle, the tarn shelf and the north slopes
current.descent: Descent is a straightforward walk/scramble reversal of the ascent line — no rappelling and no technical descent gear needed. From the Plummer Peak summit, downclimb the same class 2-3 scramble terrain back to the tarn/shelf below, staying alert on the loose rock and thin tread (most parties find the down-scramble more exposed-feeling than the ascent since you're facing outward on the steeper north slope). Rejoin the boot path back to Pinnacle Saddle, then drop onto the maintained Pinnacle Peak Trail and follow its switchbacks down through the talus/heather slopes and back into forest to the Reflection Lakes trailhead. The same hazards apply in reverse: lingering snow on the steep north-facing switchbacks just below the saddle is the most common problem spot (an ice axe or trekking poles with caution are worth carrying into July in high-snow years), and the talus sections can be slick when wet. No water past the seasonal creek around 0.6 mi from the trailhead, so plan accordingly on the way down.
current.detailed_rack: None required — this is an unroped Class 2 scramble with no fixed or removable protection used.
current.pro_needs: No protection or rope is used on this route; it is a hands-on scramble, not a roped climb.
bivy: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
current.rope_note: Class 2 easy walk-up from the Pinnacle-Plummer saddle; short rock scramble near the summit, no rope needed.

name: East Face
beta: The first pitch is the technical and psychological crux: sustained 5.9 face/dike climbing off the bergschrund with roughly 40 feet of essentially unprotectable climbing before gear appears around half height. Confident, composed 5.9 face-climbing ability and comfort well above sparse pro are essential before committing to the lead.
overview: Poltergeist Pinnacle is a slender granite tower immediately south of Mount Challenger's summit in the Northern Pickets — one of the last named summits in the range to see a first ascent. Its sole documented route, the East Face (Grade IV, 5.9), climbs a striking shield of dark granite streaked with white dikes via three pitches of sustained 5.8-5.9+ face and corner climbing (the first pitch, largely unprotected for its first ~40 feet, is the technical and psychological crux), followed by a long simul-climbed section of roughly 270 m up the connecting ridge to the summit.

current.approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FR 32, ~3,100 ft) on Trail #674. Climb steadily through forest for about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass (5,050 ft), then descend the climbers' path toward the Chilliwack River/Boundary Camp area (last reliable water for a while) before regaining elevation onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the old fire-lookout foundation/antenna remains atop Easy Peak. From Easy Ridge, contour toward Whatcom Peak's east flank to the infamous 'Imperfect Impasse' — a moat/cliff notch that often still holds snow well into summer and typically requires a short stretch of low 5th-class downclimbing or a scramble around/under a snow tunnel to cross; rope up if it looks insecure. Beyond the Impasse, climb snowfields (fog/whiteout is a real hazard here — parties have mistakenly headed for Whatcom's summit wall instead of the pass) up to Perfect Pass (~6,200 ft), the standard base camp below Whatcom Peak. Trailhead to camp is roughly 16 miles one-way with about 7,000 ft of cumulative gain — a full, long day (8-12+ hours) for a fast party, and worth splitting into two days for most. From Perfect Pass, the second-day approach crosses onto the Challenger Glacier: rope up for crevasse hazard, traverse east around Challenger Arm, and cross roughly 2.5-3 miles of upper glacier into Luna Cirque below the east side of Mt. Challenger's subsidiary summits. In lower-snow years a broken icefall blocks the direct line beneath Challenger's sub-peaks; most parties detour high above the first crevasse band (or backtrack to Challenger Arm for a lower line) to reach the base of Poltergeist Pinnacle's distinctive dike-streaked granite shield, the southernmost sub-summit between Challenger and Crooked Thumb.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge, Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier
current.descent: From the top of the route's ridge pitch, continue simulclimbing or belaying easy 5th-class terrain along the connecting ridge crest to the true summit of Mt. Challenger. This ridge traverse, not a rappel down the face just climbed, is the standard way off Poltergeist Pinnacle. From Challenger's summit, descend the mountain's standard Challenger Glacier route: downclimb or make one rappel down the short summit rock step (a compact, well-protected 5.5-5.6 wall) from fixed slings at the top. Reports differ on the rope this needs, from a 30 m rope being just enough to a 40 m rope with a few feet to spare, so carry 40 m. From the base of that rappel, rope up for glacier travel and descend the Challenger Glacier (crevasse hazard, worse late-season or in low-snow years), retracing the approach around Challenger Arm back toward Perfect Pass or a Luna Cirque camp.
current.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack: cams from small to about 3 inches, a set of nuts, and extra slings for the corner and ledge pitches; rock is generally sound and takes gear well, except the first ~40 ft of the dike-streaked shield on pitch 1, which is essentially unprotectable. Add a rope for the Challenger Glacier crossing on approach and descent.
current.pro_needs: Gear anchors throughout — the rock is sound and protects well, except the first ~40 ft of pitch 1 across the dike shield, which takes essentially no gear. Fixed anchors (bolts) are prohibited across the surrounding Stephen Mather Wilderness, so retreat and belays rely entirely on removable protection.
bivy: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak

name: Prey
beta: A series of corners, overhangs, and slabs to the top of Osprey Wall with excellent crystal pocket holds; protection is a mix of bolts and natural gear, with the third pitch fully bolted. Pitch 1 ("First Flight," 5.6) is a bolted slab ending in a chute; P2 (5.9+) climbs a right-facing corner with a roof and bolted slab; P3 (5.10c, "the money pitch") features roof systems and an arete on white marbled rock; P4 (5.9) follows a corner ramp becoming an open book (with two variations); P5 (5.10c) finishes on an arete.
overview: Prey climbs a 5-pitch (510 ft), mostly-bolted line up corners, roofs, and an arete on the right side of Osprey Wall on quality white marbled rock, highlighted by a celebrated 5.10c third pitch, the "money pitch."

current.approach: From the pullout, a short (~5-minute) woods trail leads to a large boulder/scree field at the base of the slope. From there, ascend and angle left for about 15 minutes to reach a mossy ramp system that marks the start of the wall. The route up the ramp climbs the mossy slab's far-left side, diagonaling toward the top right where a fixed rappel anchor (inspect before trusting) allows descent; a full 60m rope skips the mossy slab entirely, landing back at the scree field. Best conditions are summer when the slab is dry. Osprey Wall is a small, lightly-documented crag, so treat these approach specifics as generally reliable but not pinpoint-precise until verified on site.
current.descent: From the top of the wall, double-rope rappels (two 60 m ropes) from tree anchors on climber's left lead back down, trending slightly left to the next ledge — inspect any fixed gear before trusting it due to reported pika damage at anchors. Alternatively, descend the scree slope, using the full rope length as a handline/backup if downclimbing.
current.detailed_rack: Double ropes; ~13 quickdraws; offset cams; Totems; small nuts; long slings for the wandering corner and roof systems.
current.pro_needs: Mixed bolted and gear-protected climbing (P3 is fully bolted); bring offset cams, Totems, and small nuts for the corner/roof pitches, plus long slings to manage rope drag, and double ropes for the descent.

name: Primal Scream
beta: A granite ridge climb with lichened overlaps, gardened dirt-filled cracks and clean tactile smears on low-angle granite; the crux comes late, on pitch 9, with an S-curved crack and bulge with smearing moves to chain anchors. Modern bolted anchors added in 2023 made the route rappel-able for the first time.
overview: An old-school, 12-pitch alpine ridge ramble up the crest of the South Face's central buttress, established in 1997 well before the wall's newer bolted lines, sharing its final three pitches with Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer.

current.approach: From the grassy saddle bivy, cross class 4 ramps to a shallow dihedral with a small tree, then continue to a dirt ledge at the base of a short wall marking the start.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
current.descent: Rappel the line of ascent using the 2023-installed modern bolted anchors; the upper three pitches share anchors with Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer.
current.detailed_rack: Standard rack to 3", with doubles in the 0.75"-2" range recommended for the gardened crack pitches.
current.pro_needs: A mix of natural gear in dirt-filled cracks on the lower/middle pitches and 2023-installed bolted anchors at every belay for protection and descent.

name: South Ridge / McAllister Glacier
beta: Primus Peak's difficulty lies almost entirely in its remoteness and glacier approach rather than technical climbing. From this side the summit itself is class 2-3 snow and talus above the North Klawatti Glacier, reached after a short rock step at the McAllister-Klawatti notch. Most parties treat it as a 3-4 day trip with a high camp near Klawatti Col. A harder 'North Ridge' variant (5.6 trad, loose and exposed) exists for parties wanting technical climbing.
overview: The South Ridge / McAllister Glacier route approaches Primus from the opposite (Cascade River Road/Eldorado) side of the mountain rather than via Thunder Creek, crossing the Eldorado, Inspiration, and North Klawatti/McAllister Glaciers through the Klawatti–Austera high country. It's commonly climbed as part of the Inspiration Traverse or combined with Austera, Klawatti, and/or Tricouni Peaks rather than as a standalone objective — Primus ranks among the most remote of Washington's Bulger List summits.

current.approach: Trailhead is the Eldorado Creek climbers' trailhead on Cascade River Road, roughly mile 20 out of Marblemount, at about 2,100 ft. From the parking pullout, backtrack a short distance downstream along the road to find a log or braided crossing of the North Fork Cascade River; ford/cross and pick up the unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path on the far bank, angling up through heavy timber. This boot path is steep and root-laced, gaining roughly 1,800-1,900 ft through forest before breaking out at a boulder field around 4,000 ft; follow cairns and the intermittent trail on the right side of the talus (roughly 1,000 vertical ft of boulder-hopping) up into the open meadows of Eldorado Creek/Eldorado Basin. From the basin, continue up benches toward the toe of the Eldorado Glacier (often called Eldorado Camp, ~6,000-7,500 ft) - this is a reasonable first-night camp and the last reliable running water before the ice cap. Rope up here: the Eldorado Glacier is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year, and parties have needed to weave crevasse mazes even on the standard line. From upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col (~7,800 ft) - this leg is long, exposed to whiteout (several parties describe navigating the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility), and is the standard second camp for the Eldorado Ice Cap traverse that accesses Primus. From Klawatti Col camp, the climb of Primus itself is a summit-day push: down-climb or make a short (~50 ft) rappel through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier. Rope up, traverse north and then east below the south side of Austera's east ridge, descending to round the end of that ridge near 6,800 ft onto the North Klawatti Glacier, and cross it (probing for hidden crevasses - this section has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility) to the foot of Primus's south face. Unrope and climb snow ramps and then talus up the face, moving right onto the south ridge for the last couple of hundred feet to the 8,508 ft summit. The trailhead sits about 6,400 ft below the summit, and the round trip takes two to three days or more; mid-to-late summer (glacier bridges more consolidated, less whiteout risk) is the recommended window.
approach_variant_names: The far end of the Eldorado ice cap: five glaciers and a notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col
Thunder Creek and the Borealis Glacier: the east ridge from Lucky Pass
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down-climb the summit talus back to the North Klawatti Glacier, rope back up, and re-cross the glacier (same crevasse-probing caution as the approach) to the base of the McAllister-Klawatti notch. Regaining the notch back up to Klawatti Col camp is normally a climb/scramble rather than a rappel; the technical crux of the day - the short ~50 ft step between the notch and the glacier - is the one spot parties commonly fix a hand line or short rappel on the way down from the ridge, then climb the same step (with a boost from a partner or a fixed line) on the return leg. Primus's west-ridge line has a similar ~8,200 ft notch requiring a roughly 50 ft rappel to regain the glacier when descending, which lines up with an account of a party rappelling at the McAllister-Klawatti col - treat this as a single, short technical rappel rather than a multi-pitch rap descent. A single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient (a doubled 30m or single 60m easily covers 50-60 ft); anchors are natural (slings on horns/blocks) rather than bolted, since this is remote glaciated terrain with no fixed hardware. From Klawatti Col camp, the multi-day exit reverses the approach: back across the Inspiration Glacier (whiteout and crevasse hazard again), down the Eldorado Glacier, through Eldorado Basin, down the boulder field and timber climbers' path, and back across the North Fork Cascade River to the trailhead. Watch for softening glacier bridges and increased rockfall/scree looseness on the boulder-field descent in the afternoon heat.
current.detailed_rack: No rock gear required for the scramble; full glacier rescue equipment essential.
current.pro_needs: None on the scramble; glacier protection as conditions dictate.
bivy: Klawatti Col camp, Eldorado ice-cap traverse approach

name: Project Crack
beta: A wiggly crack in mossy rock. Climb through a moss-covered corner ledge, then mossy face climbing to a moss-covered summit jug. Bolts mentioned in older descriptions were not visible on a recent visit, likely buried under moss -- treat as a natural-gear/trad line with a chain anchor at the top.
overview: A moss-lined, traditionally-protected crack line at the far end of the East Face, notable for heavy moss coverage rather than technical difficulty.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive east on I-90 to Snoqualmie Pass and take Exit 54, crossing to the north side of the freeway before turning onto FR 4832, then following it onto FR 4934 to the small trailhead pullout. On foot, cross the road and hike up a spur road for about 15 minutes to a flat bench, then pick up a cairned trail heading north into the forest to a rocky area, staying on the main climber's trail through a short, steeper forest section to reach the crag — roughly 25-30 minutes total from the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is generally expected for parking at national forest trailheads in this corridor.
current.descent: From the top, lower directly off the fixed chain anchor to the ground with a single 60m rope; no walk-off is required.
current.detailed_rack: Gear to 3 inches (single rack). Reported bolts from older published descriptions were not found/visible on a recent ascent -- come prepared to protect it as a natural line. Chain anchor at the top.
rack: Trad rack to 3 inches (single set of cams)
current.pro_needs: Trad gear to 3"; do not count on bolts even though older descriptions mention them.
current.rope_note: The name and 5.9+ grade suggest a crack line — the East Face sector does include at least one trad route, so this may require actual cam/nut protection rather than pure bolted sport gear.

name: Sail Away
beta: P1 ('The Onramp', 5.5) romps up an easy 5th-class left-leaning slab to a pine-covered ledge. P2 ('The Superflake', 5.9) climbs a steep flake system tapering to an airy spire. P3 (5.9) steps right into a dihedral. P4 (5.10-) tackles a slightly overhanging crack with good gear to an angled ledge. P5 ('Gemini Cracks', 5.10) offers tight, baggy hand cracks with a traverse option. P6 ('Sail Headwall', 5.11) finishes on an elegant, slightly overhanging crack progressing from thin fingers to off-width.
overview: A six-pitch 5.11 route about 20 yards left of Solid Gold, climbing an easy slab onramp into a series of increasingly steep flakes and cracks, finished by an overhanging 'sail-shaped' headwall crack.

approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass
Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
current.descent: The last pitch ends on easier ground on the west side of the sail-shaped headwall. From there the Solid Gold rappel anchors are close by. Make two rappels from those anchors, then walk off down the back (north) side and scramble around to the base of the south face.
current.detailed_rack: Triple cams up to 1in, doubles up to 4in, optional #5/#6 cams for the off-width finish.
current.pro_needs: Triples through 1 inch, doubles through 4 inches; #5 and #6 cams optional. Finger-to-2-inch gear sees the most use.

name: Standard Route / Southeast Scramble
beta: From the end of the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail, an unmaintained but cairned climbers' path continues up the long south ridge through forest, brush, and boulder fields to timberline. The route then traverses below steep cliffs on the peak's east side (prone to sliding) before climbing to the saddle between Pinnacle and Pyramid Peaks. From the saddle it's an easy walk to Pyramid's summit. The route's overall difficulty is Class 3 scrambling, though most of the elevation gain is Class 1-2 hiking with only short harder sections.
overview: Pyramid Peak (7,189 ft) is the northernmost summit in a dramatic chain above Diablo Lake that also includes Colonial Peak, Snowfield Peak, Paul Bunyan's Stump, and Pinnacle Peak, all linked by one long, south-trending ridge and reached via the shared Pyramid Lake climbers' trail. Its steep, pyramid-shaped north face — rising roughly 6,400 ft above the Skagit River in just 2.5 miles — is one of the signature views from the Diablo Lake Overlook and Diablo Dam on the North Cascades Highway. Built of the range's characteristic banded gneiss, the peak is more intimidating in profile than in practice: the standard route is a long, sustained Class 3 scramble with a short snow finish to a broad, easy summit, not a technical climb. It was first climbed in 1931 by Seattle Mountaineers William Degenhardt and Herbert Strandberg, and sits within the North Cascades National Park Service Complex (Ross Lake NRA / NP South Unit).

current.approach: From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 126.8 (about 6.5 miles east of Newhalem, on the north shoulder just east of Diablo Lake), cross the highway to the signed Pyramid Lake trailhead (roughly 1,150–1,200 ft) at the base of Pyramid Creek's cascades. The maintained, National Park Service-built tread climbs steadily through second-growth and remnant old-growth forest (some sections show past fire scarring), fords Pyramid Creek on rock/log around the 0.9-mile mark near a stand of old cedars — this is the last reliable water before the summit push, so treat it here — and continues switchbacking up to Pyramid Lake at 2.1 miles with about 1,500 ft of gain (lake sits around 2,600–2,700 ft). Pyramid Lake itself, a small deep tarn dammed by an ancient landslide, is closed to camping within a half-mile, so parties splitting the route into two days push on before making camp. Past the lake the maintained trail ends and a boot-built, cairned climbers' path takes over — tread is intermittent and easy to lose, especially in early-season snow or whiteout. At the lake's outlet, bear right (west) over a small rock knob and through a brief dip, then the path turns and climbs steeply and directly up the ridge, gaining on the order of 3,000+ ft over the next couple of miles through brush, root-pull sections, and low-grade scrambling. Partway up, look for a boulder field below a steep knob; cairns route around it via a brushy path on its south side. Above treeline the cairned path crosses slabs and heather benches past a couple of small tarns (a possible late-season water source) before the route splits: climbers bound for Pyramid continue up onto the ridge below Paul Bunyan's Stump and traverse below/around Pinnacle Peak to the saddle between Pinnacle and Pyramid, while those bound for Colonial Peak instead drop left onto a cedar bench into the Colonial Creek basin. East-facing snowfields and a notch/traverse just below the summit ridge hold snow well into summer, so carry an ice axe (crampons in early season) even in July–August. From the Pinnacle–Pyramid saddle, the final stretch to the summit is an easy, non-technical hike/scramble over talus and lingering snow patches — the summit itself is broad and nearly flat. The genuine crux of the day is route-finding above the lake: the bootpath through the boulder field, timberline benches, and the notch below the summit ridge is where parties most often go off-route.
approach_variant_names: Pyramid Lake climbers' path
current.descent: This is a full walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling anywhere on the standard route. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb back through the notch and short exposed traverse below the summit ridge (the one spot worth facing in and taking carefully, especially if icy or holding old snow), then pick back down past the false high points toward the Pinnacle–Pyramid saddle and the cairned bootpath. Below treeline, parties note the path effectively forks on the boulder-field/brush section: a 'climbers-right' line with easier, short class 3 moves is commonly used on the ascent, while a steeper, somewhat more exposed 'climbers-left' line sometimes gets taken (intentionally or by accident) on the way down — stay on cairns rather than following the first boot-track you see, since the exposed variant is not the preferred descent. In early to mid-season, the remnant snowfields on the ridge below Paul Bunyan's Stump offer glissade options for parties carrying ice axes and comfortable self-arresting; by August those slopes are mostly bare talus and it's a straightforward scramble/hike back down to Pyramid Lake, rejoining the maintained trail for the final 2.1 miles and ~1,500 ft of descent back to the SR-20 trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed for the standard scramble. A rope is optional insurance some parties carry for the exposed traverse beneath the cliffs, but it is not standard practice on this route.
current.pro_needs: Mostly Class 3-4 scrambling; a short rope and a few slings are optional for the exposed summit steps.
bivy: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
current.rope_note: No glacier on this route, but steep snowfields below Pinnacle Peak and the summit ridge linger into summer - carry an ice axe (crampons early season); final ridge/summit is a Class 3 rock scramble, typically unroped.

name: Ragged Edge
beta: From the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, an obvious ledge system cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft, starting at a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier. The climbing is sustained low-5th-class rock with the crux exposed traverse pitch reported on pitch 5 (some parties also flag a 5.7 slab on pitch 2); belays are a mix of fixed (bolted/pin) anchors and gear anchors atop pitches 1 and 3. No rappels are needed — parties walk off. Popular enough that other Vesper lines (e.g. True Grit) are sometimes used as a less-crowded backup.
overview: Ragged Edge climbs the right side of Vesper's clean north face via shallow corners, flakes and slabs, established by Darin Berdinka and Gene Pires on August 18, 2013. It's the most popular moderate line on the wall — low-angle, well-featured 5.7 climbing on ~700 ft of granite, capped by an exposed, aptly-named finish right along the edge of the face.

current.approach: Same trailhead and trail as True Grit: Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway, through second-growth forest and an early creek crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish (log crossing, harder in high runoff), up through Wirtz Basin and out onto open, cairned talus, then through Headlee Pass (~4,720 ft, 2.7 mi, loose rock/rockfall exposure in the narrow couloir) and down to Vesper Creek and Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~5,000 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain) — the last dependable water. From the lake the maintained trail fades; cross the outlet and follow an obvious talus ridgeline up to the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, the small summit just northeast of Vesper. From there a slightly improbable but well-trodden heather ledge system (goat trail through it) cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft to a small notch overlooking the remnant Vesper Glacier, where the route starts. This traverse crosses steep, exposed heather that's treacherous when wet and typically holds snow into mid-to-late summer, so an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying into early summer. Plan on 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the climb.
approach_variant_names: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
current.descent: No rappels are required — Ragged Edge tops out at or very near Vesper's summit, and the standard exit is a walk-off down the peak's east side/East Ridge back toward the Vesper-Wolf saddle, then down to Vesper Lake and out the Sunrise Mine Trail. The descent is class 2-3 scrambling/talus, occasionally holding snow into early summer (ice axe useful then), and is fast relative to the climb — most parties are back at the saddle and lake within an hour or two of topping out, with the whole car-to-car day often wrapping up in well under 12 hours. Watch for loose rock on the upper descent slopes, especially with parties above or below.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles of cams .5-1", singles of .2, .3, .4, 2", and 3", plus a set of small/micro nuts; a single 60m rope is sufficient. Belays mix fixed (bolted/pin) anchors with gear anchors built atop pitches 1 and 3.
current.pro_needs: Standard trad rack to 3"; the route is a mix of gear, bolts, and pins, and was retro-bolted in places in August 2013.
bivy: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
current.rope_note: 6-pitch route (5.5-5.7); fixed anchors at most belays, gear belays atop P1 and P3; P5 is most gear-hungry pitch.

name: Ragged Ridge
beta: Typically approached via Easy Pass and Fisher Creek to a high camp on Mesahchie's south shoulder, then done as either a long single-day push (~13-14 hrs car-to-car) or a 2-day trip across the four 8,000+ ft summits (Kitling Peak to the east is sometimes added). No roped rock climbing is required, but the terrain is loose, exposed, and route-finding-intensive.
overview: A rugged, mostly non-technical scramble traverse linking the summits of Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah, and Cosho Peaks along Ragged Ridge above Easy Pass, involving sustained Class 3-4 terrain, glacier crossings, and an exposed 'red ledge' passage.

current.approach: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20, hike the Easy Pass Trail about 3.5 miles and roughly 2,900 ft to Easy Pass, about 6,500 ft. Most parties then leave the trail and sidehill west along the south side of the ridge on grassy benches around 6,600-6,800 ft, crossing many small gullies and buttresses; a large gully with a waterfall just before the basin needs a short descent of steep scree. The usual high camp is in the basin just south of Mesahchie Peak at about 6,600-6,700 ft, roughly five hours from the car. The alternative is to follow the trail down the far side of the pass into the Fisher Creek basin near 5,100 ft and climb off-trail back up to the same camp. From camp, climb northwest to the Mesahchie-Katsuk saddle to start the traverse.
current.descent: Trip reports consistently recommend dropping off the ridge to the Fisher Creek trail (roughly 2-2.5 hrs from the Cosho/west end) rather than attempting a high traverse back at 7,000+ ft, which is described as slow, exposed sidehilling through 'awfulness'; from Fisher Creek, follow the maintained trail back over Easy Pass to the trailhead.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection or roped rock climbing is typically needed; a rope, light rack, and glacier gear are prudent for the Katsuk/Kimtah glacier crossings and any unexpected short technical steps.
bivy: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
current.rope_note: Mostly Class 3-4 scrambling along Ragged Ridge with brief low-5th-class steps; a light rope covers the Katsuk and Kimtah glacier crossings and any short step a party wants protected, and most of the ridge is climbed unroped.

name: Raven Ridge Standard Route (Libby Lake Gully-Ridge)
beta: From the Libby Lake Trailhead, hike the well-graded Libby Creek/Libby Lake Trail roughly 5.1–5.5 miles and about 3,185–3,210 ft of gain to Libby Lake (~7,618–7,640 ft). From the lake, locate the loose talus gully that accesses the east-west-oriented ridge (some parties report two gully options near the lake's south end; the standard line rises about 900 ft). The gully is loose and rockfall-prone — favor the climber's-left wall for firmer rock and to reduce hazard to parties below. Once on the ridge crest, an exposed Class 2–3 scramble of roughly half a mile leads toward the summit block, which has a short, unavoidable, no-fall Class 4 move (some reports mention a small tunnel feature en route). USGS topo maps mislabel the western "Libby" summit as the high point (8,580 ft); the true, higher summit is the eastern peak at 8,572 ft. The true east summit is also known as Corax Peak; a separate, lower point sits just west of the main summit saddle. Strong parties often continue the ridge traverse north to Hoodoo Peak, which adds a long exposed Class 4 section and a 5.7 overhanging boulder problem best protected with a short rope.
overview: The standard route follows the Libby Lake Trail to alpine Libby Lake, then climbs a steep, very loose ~900-ft talus gully to gain the Raven Ridge crest, finishing with an exposed Class 3–4 scramble east along the ridge to the true (east) summit at 8,572 ft.

current.approach: From Twisp, drive WA-20 east a short distance to WA-153, then south on WA-153 to Libby Creek Road (County Road 1045), about 1.4 miles south of Carlton. Turn right and follow Libby Creek Road about 2.5 miles, turn left onto Forest Road 43 for about 5.1 miles, left onto Forest Road 4340 for about 1.2 miles, right onto Forest Road 4340-700 for about 1.5 miles, and left onto Forest Road 4340-750 for about 0.9 mile to the Libby Lake Trailhead (4,400–4,430 ft; roadside parking for roughly 10 vehicles, no toilet or potable water). From the trailhead, follow Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake, watching for trail damage (root holes) from the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire between roughly miles 0.8 and 2.5. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail at about 7,170 ft, used by some parties as a base camp.
approach_variant_names: Libby Creek road and Trail #415 to Libby Lake
From the Crater Creek road and the lake basin, gaining the crest from the south-east
current.descent: There is no separate descent line for the standard route — parties reverse their ascent. The crux of the descent is the loose gully: move deliberately, stay to the climber's-left (looking downhill) on more solid rock where possible, and be conscious that dislodged rock can strike other parties below. No fixed rappel anchors exist on the standard line (a rappel station has been reported on the connecting ridge toward Libby Peak/Hoodoo Peak, not on the standard Raven Ridge summit route). Retrace the trail from Libby Lake back to the Libby Lake Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed protection or technical rack is needed for the standard scrambling line. Parties planning to continue the connecting ridge toward Hoodoo Peak (or wanting a safety net for the Class 4 summit move) sometimes carry a short 30–60 m rope or a sling, since a rappel station exists on that connector near a near-vertical step.
current.pro_needs: None fixed on the standard route; an optional short rope/sling covers the exposed Class 4 summit move or the Hoodoo Peak ridge connector.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Approach via Pacific Crest Trail north from Exit 52, following Commonwealth Creek trail to the base of the mountain. The final 1,000-1,100 feet ascends the west-facing slope at 30-40 degrees inclination. Most loose rock has been removed by frequent traffic. South-facing sections feature more solid red volcanic slabs. Winter ascents are possible with snow coverage on the southwest ridge when avalanche conditions are stable.
overview: Red Mountain (5,890 ft) is the distinctive rust-red peak rising above Commonwealth Basin, 3 miles north of Snoqualmie Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. One of the popular 'Snoqualmie Ten,' it's a non-technical but genuinely loose scramble: the red color comes from iron-oxide staining on heavily fractured volcanic rock, which is notoriously crumbly and rockfall-prone despite the peak's benign reputation as a walk-up.

current.approach: Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT trailhead) at Snoqualmie Pass West, reached via I-90 Exit 52 — this is the road-access endpoint; from the trailhead the hike itself begins on the newer rerouted Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Follow the PCT for roughly 2–2.5 miles of well-graded, well-maintained trail through old-growth forest with blueberry and salmonberry understory. At the signed junction, leave the PCT and turn left onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, following it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek in the basin, which is the one reliable natural water source on the approach (treat before drinking) — carry enough water above this point since the final scramble slopes are dry. As the trail levels out near a small tarn/pond below Red Mountain's west slope, watch for a cairn planted in the middle of the path — this marks the scramble takeoff point where you leave the maintained trail. An alternate, rougher approach follows the older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin Trail starting about 20 yards up from the parking lot, switchbacking directly up into the basin and rejoining near the same trail split (bear right toward Red Pass); it's shorter but harder to follow and not recommended in poor visibility. From the cairn, pick up a boot path climbing the west slope; the track is intermittent and easy to lose on scree, so stay close to the ridge crest on climber's right (south) if you're unsure of the line. The final roughly 900 ft over the last half mile is the crux of the approach: a 30–40° slope of fractured red (iron-stained) rock, loose scree, heather, and scattered alpine trees, alternating Class 2 and low Class 3 scrambling with no real exposure — hands are needed intermittently but it's non-technical. This upper slope holds snow into early summer and can present avalanche/glissade hazard in spring conditions; by mid-to-late summer it's typically dry but still loose and slick when wet.
approach_variant_names: PCT and Commonwealth Creek trail to the cairn by the tarn, then the west-slope boot path
current.descent: No rope or rappelling is used on the standard route — this is a pure walk/scramble descent. Most parties reverse the ascent line down the west-slope boot path back to the cairn and Commonwealth Creek Trail, then retrace the Commonwealth Creek Trail and PCT back to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend via the southwest ridge crest before dropping back into the boot-path drainage, which can offer more solid footing than the loose central scree the boot path sometimes follows — either line rejoins the same trail system before the pond. The overriding descent hazard is loose, fractured rock underfoot (a helmet is strongly recommended for the whole party, not just the leader, since Red Mountain's red rock is notoriously fractured and easy to kick loose onto climbers below); keep the group tight and avoid spreading out on the open scree. Do not attempt to traverse east/south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Catwalk as a shortcut — that terrain quickly becomes Class 3/4 and cliffs out without a rope. Once back on the boot path, staying close to the ridge crest on the way down (rather than cutting straight down the gut of the scree slope) both preserves the trail and reduces rockfall risk to other parties.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack required.
current.pro_needs: None — no rack, rope, or protection needed; this is unroped Class 2-3 scrambling on both standard lines.

name: Red Zinger
beta: 5 bolts to chains. Approach to Megadike North 1.1-1.2 miles past Middle Point Ridge Trailhead.
overview: Short moderate sport climb on Megadike North.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: pull over at 1.1 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, at the spot on the left (SE side) where a dirt road joins the pavement, or drive on to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
current.descent: Lower from the chain anchor on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: 5 bolts to chains.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (5 bolts).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike North (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given Megadike North's walls up to ~120ft.

name: Redtail Arete
beta: Long moderate slabby arete. Bolts to anchors at top.
overview: Moderate slabby arete on south edge of a pinnacle known as Black Tooth on Megadike South.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike South: drive 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and park on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river. Scramble up the steep hillside on the NW side of the road above the bridge abutment, then continue uphill along the dike to a passable gully.
current.descent: Lower from the anchor at top on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: Bolted route to anchors at top; standard sport rack for a 60 ft slab.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike South (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given crag-wide walls up to 120-140ft.

name: NW Ridge
beta: From a high camp at roughly 7,500 ft on the lower ridge, the route follows a long, stable, lightly-vegetated boulder ridge to the North Summit, from which two rappels on the west side regain the ridge crest. Beyond, two main gendarmes block easy passage; each is climbed at about 5.1-5.2. The line appears sensible as a route; it sees very little traffic. Parties can bypass the technical sections by staying lower on the west slope, avoiding the vertical sections but missing the ridge's technical interest.
overview: A rarely-climbed alpine ridge line up Remmel's long ridge north of the summit above Remmel Lake, combining sections of 3rd-class scrambling with short 5.1-5.2 pitches over two gendarmes.

current.approach: From Remmel Lake, bushwhack roughly 2 miles up the forested slope due south of the lake, through mosquito-infested timber and subalpine bog, to a high camp at treeline (~7,500 ft) on the lower NW ridge.
approach_variant_names: Andrews Creek to Remmel Lake
Chewuch River trail to Remmel Lake
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the upper ridge scrambling to the first gendarme, rappel its west side, continue down the ridge to the second gendarme, rappel it, then scramble down and around the west slope on boulders and scree, bypassing the North Summit, back to the high camp at ~7,500 ft; from there retrace the bushwhack to Remmel Lake.
current.detailed_rack: Small set of nuts and cams to mid-size, a few slings and draws for the short low-5th-class sections, and enough webbing or cord to back up natural rappel anchors around the gendarmes.
rack: Light trad rack: cams and stoppers to ~2in
3x 60cm webbing for flake/horn protection and simple anchors
One 50-60 m single rope for the two short rappels
current.pro_needs: A light alpine rack — stoppers and cams to about 2 inches — protects the short low-5th-class gendarme pitches, plus slings and cord for backing up natural anchors on the granite; fixed anchors are unlikely on this rarely-climbed line. A single 50-60 m rope is enough for the short rappels.
bivy: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
current.rope_note: No indexed route-specific gear list could be found online, and the published coverage for this peak is not available digitally. Recommendation reflects a light rack for a low-grade (5.2) alpine granite ridge; many parties simul-climb or solo given the easy grade.

name: Southeast Slope (Standard Route)
beta: Remmel is a classic Pasayten peak-bagging objective: a big, remote walk-up rather than a technical climb. Most parties backpack in via one of three trailheads (Thirtymile/Chewuch River Trail to Four Point Lake, the shorter but rougher Andrews Creek approach, or the Cathedral Driveway) and then follow an obvious boot path up open talus and meadow slopes to the broad summit.
overview: The standard route follows a well-established unofficial climbers' trail up Remmel's southeast slope from Four Point Lake — a long, remote but non-technical Class 1-2 talus-and-meadow walk-up to the summit.

current.approach: From the Thirtymile Trailhead (end of FR 51, ~3,400 ft) or the Andrews Creek Trailhead (on FR 51 at the end of the pavement, ~3,050 ft), hike into the Pasayten Wilderness. Via Thirtymile: follow the Chewuch River Trail and Four Point Creek Trail to Four Point Lake (6,850 ft), then pick up the abandoned Coleman Ridge Trail; at roughly 7,070 ft a cairn marks the point to leave the trail and climb open meadow/talus up-valley to the summit on a well-trodden unofficial path. Via Andrews Creek: hike the Andrews Creek Trail roughly 9-11 miles (crossing heavy deadfall in an old 2003 burn in the lower miles) to a low saddle between Remmel and Coleman Ridge, then contour the west side of Coleman Ridge to reach the same upper slopes; alternatively continue to Andrews Pass (~6,700 ft) and climb one of several Class 3 west-facing gullies directly to the summit ridge.
current.descent: Downclimb the talus/meadow boot path back to the Coleman Ridge Trail junction near 7,070 ft, then follow the trail back to Four Point Lake (or, via the Andrews Creek line, back down the Class 3 gullies or around via the Coleman Ridge contour) and out the approach trail to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: None. This is a non-technical Class 1 walk-up on the standard route — no rope or rack is carried.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Parties typically approach via Twisp River Road to either the Reynolds Creek drainage (shortest, most direct) or the Williams Creek trail, then climb open basins and snowfields on the southeast side of the peak to a saddle/notch below the summit. From there, a Class 2-3 gully leads to the ridge crest, followed by a short, somewhat exposed Class 3 scramble on solid granite to the true (southeast) summit. Longer alternative approaches traverse in from Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge, or from the west via Bridge Creek and Stehekin ('the back way'), but all eventually join the same southeast-side summit scramble rather than offering a genuinely distinct technical line.
overview: Reynolds Peak (8,517 ft) is a high, horned, twin-summited peak on the divide between the Twisp River and Lake Chelan country, within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness (Methow Mountains, North Cascades), about 6 miles northeast of Stehekin. It is one of the most visually striking summits in the Chelan Sawtooth range even though it isn't the highest. The south summit is the true high point; a subsidiary North Peak (8,384 ft) sits 0.3 mile to the north and is easy to mistake for the top since it's reached first and is non-technical. Rock is a sound tonalitic orthogneiss. Isolation to the nearest higher peak (Oval Peak) is about 8.5 miles, and local relief above Reynolds Creek exceeds 3,500 ft within a mile, giving the peak its prominent, rugged look from the Twisp River valley.

current.approach: From the Reynolds Creek Trailhead (~3,100–3,170 ft, reached via Forest Road 4435, which crosses the Twisp River near Mystery Campground before the Spur 4435-015 turnoff to the trailhead), the route follows Reynolds Creek Trail #402, an unmaintained, primitive Forest Service trail entering the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. Trail #402 climbs steadily through mixed conifer forest along Reynolds Creek for roughly 3 miles to the confluence where the South Fork of Reynolds Creek meets the main creek (approx. 4,800–5,000 ft) — parties describe scooting across a downed log to make this crossing, which can be a genuine ford in high early-season flow. This confluence is the last reliable, easy water source before the upper basin, so fill up here. Beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread and follow the South Fork drainage, staying roughly 50 ft above the creek to avoid the worst brush and log-hopping directly in the streambed. Expect about 2 miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber, and a boot-path/game-trail tread that comes and goes — this is the route-finding crux of the approach, and parties specifically flag the numerous fallen logs and dense brush here. The drainage opens into a broad talus/scree basin around 5,500–5,700 ft directly below Reynolds Peak's southeast face and the gully/snowfield leading to its east ridge. This basin and the gully above it hold snow well into summer in most years, so carry an ice axe (and traction in early season) even on an otherwise dry-looking late-summer day. From the basin, ascend the scree, talus, and (seasonally) snow of the SE slopes/gully to a saddle/notch on the peak's east ridge, then finish with a short, exposed class 2–3 scramble (occasionally reported as harder, class 3–4, depending on snow coverage) up sound granite summit rocks to the 8,517 ft high point. An alternate, more scenic but similarly long approach exists via Williams Creek Trail and War Creek Ridge from a different Twisp River Road trailhead, but Reynolds Creek Trail #402 is the standard, shorter line. The longer Williams Creek/War Creek Ridge alternative can be combined into a loop with Abernathy Peak or Twisp Pass, running roughly 24 miles round trip with about 8,300 ft of cumulative gain.
approach_variant_names: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge
Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no rappelling on the standard route. Downclimb the class 2–3 summit rocks back to the saddle/notch on the east ridge, then descend the scree, talus, and snow gully back into the SE basin at ~5,500–5,700 ft. When the gully still holds good snow (common well into summer), this section glissades or plunge-steps quickly; once it melts out to bare scree/talus later in the season it becomes a slower, loose descent — go one at a time through any group to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below. From the basin, pick up the boot path along the South Fork's climber's-right bank back to the log crossing at the South Fork/main Reynolds Creek confluence (~4,800–5,000 ft), then follow Reynolds Creek Trail #402 the remaining ~3 miles of forest trail back to the Reynolds Creek Trailhead. This is a full retrace/walk-off descent with no fixed anchors or rappel stations reported anywhere on the standard route; treat any exposed class 3 downclimbing on the summit rocks with care rather than as a rappel substitute.
current.detailed_rack: Not a technical rock climb — most parties solo the Class 2-3 terrain, but a short (30m) rope with a few slings/runners is worth carrying to protect the exposed Class 3 step below the summit with a running belay.
current.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
current.rope_note: Class 3-4 scramble, non-technical except a few hundred feet of 3rd/4th class near the true (South) summit; no rope used in standard dry-condition ascents.

name: Ride the Lightning
beta: Sport-and-trad alpine climb on the south face with quality climbing on lower pitches transitioning to chossy rock mid-route before improving toward the summit. Bolted belay anchors on initial pitches; natural protection higher. The opening pitches below the roof are the route's best sections.
overview: A 7-pitch alpine rock route on the 800-foot south wall featuring face climbing below prominent roof features and a mix of bolted and gear-protected pitches. Initial pitches are the best climbing; the route deteriorates higher with loose rock but improves again on pitch 5.

current.approach: From Naches, take US-12 west roughly 23 miles to just past the Rimrock Lake Dam, then turn south onto Tieton Reservoir Road (FR-1200). For the popular rock routes on the eastern cliffs, park in one of the pullouts along Tieton Road near a spring marked by a split-rail fence and follow the steep climbers' trail uphill to the base of the routes. To reach the summit via the non-technical Southwest Ridge, continue on FR-1200 to the South Fork/campground turnoff, park near the restroom area, and hike cross-country, following criss-crossing boot-paths while staying on the ridge crest until it becomes an established path to the summit block. The area melts out quickly and is climbable from May through November.
approach_variant_names: Tieton Road spring and the climbers' trail
current.descent: From the summit area, walk climber's left to an obvious gully. Descend via this gully with one rappel required midway (approximately 30 feet). This is the standard descent used by most parties. Ensure you have adequate rope for any rappel anchors encountered.
current.detailed_rack: Carry a single set of cams and nuts; this should suffice for the route. Bring a dozen quickdraws or carabiners for the bolted sections. Longer slings useful for natural anchors and equalizing pieces.
rack: Single rack of cams and nuts
current.pro_needs: Single rack with standard cams and nuts; a dozen draws for bolted sections. Initial pitches have bolted anchors; upper pitches rely on gear placement.
current.rope_note: The reported rack is a single rack, a dozen draws and some longer slings. Bolted belays on the lower 4-5 pitches with trad protection needed through crack sections higher up.

name: Ridge Traverse from East Fury
beta: Once you have reached the summit of East Fury, you may continue to West Fury via this traverse. The traverse is a series of gendarmes and towers with a combination of scrambling and low 5th class rock. The descent off East Fury to the low saddle is on very loose Class 2-3 boulders. There are three towers you must climb up and over before making the final ascent to the summit of West Fury. A 50-60 meter rope is recommended at the very least for rappelling the 4th and low 5th class areas you have climbed.
overview: A wild and exposed scramble traverse connecting East Fury (8,322 ft) to West Fury (8,305 ft), involving three main towers with Class 2-4 descent to saddle and Class 4-5 climbing on towers. This is the standard method of traversing between the two peaks and involves significant exposure, loose rock, and dangerous rappels.

current.approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead and walk down to Ross Lake, where most parties take the paid water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing rather than walking the lakeshore trail. From the landing it is about 9.4 miles of nearly flat old-growth trail up the Big Beaver valley to Luna Camp, the usual first night. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of where Access Creek comes in, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade. Then climb the north side of Access Creek on a faint, brushy climbers' path through Access Creek basin, up the south gully and around the south side of Luna Peak to Luna Col, the usual high camp. From Luna Col, follow the ridge toward Fury over class 3 ground with many short ups and downs. Drop to traverse heather slopes on its south side to the Southeast Glacier near 6,700 ft, then climb the right side of the glacier to steeper snow and a possible bergschrund below East Fury's summit, where the traverse to the West Peak begins. Allow three to five days for the round trip. The Luna Fire closure has shut the Big Beaver Trail from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, including Luna Camp, and bars cross-country travel from the closed trail; check the park's current fire closures before planning.
approach_variant_names: Climb East Fury first; the traverse starts on its summit
current.descent: Descend the towers you climbed by reversing the route and setting rappels off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock. Each rappel down makes retreat progressively more difficult. Once off the traverse, descend the east side of East Fury to the saddle on loose Class 2-3 talus, then descend the Southeast Glacier back to Luna Col and the main Access Creek drainage.
current.detailed_rack: A modest rock climbing rack is essential due to poor anchor placements throughout. Bring 1-2 sets of small cams (0.4-1.5 inches) and a set of nuts for protection and rappel anchors. Many parties report difficulty finding solid rock for gear placement; natural features (trees, rocks) may be used for anchors where possible.
current.pro_needs: Protection is difficult to place due to chossy, loose granite. Many climbing parties find it nearly impossible to establish solid anchor points and often rely on natural features or accept marginal protection. Rappels are typically established using multiple strands and directional placements to increase security.
bivy: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
current.rope_note: A 50-60 m rope at minimum, for rappelling the 4th- and low-5th-class sections between the three towers. Plan on building and leaving anchors: the rock is chossy, solid placements are scarce, and the rappels on this traverse go off poor-quality anchors - so carry slings and rings to back them up. Each rappel you make on the way across makes retreat progressively harder.

name: Roan Wall - Center Stage
beta: Climbs the middle of Roan Wall via a 5.8 bolted slab approach pitch, a 5.4 approach pitch, sustained 5.9-5.10 edge and face pitches, and a 5.11a crux slab pitch (P7), finishing with mixed 5.9-5.10- climbing. All belays feature brand-new double-ring stainless-steel bolted anchors. An enormously overhung boulder (Martha's Place) sits near the base and offers a good camp/bivy spot.
overview: A 10-pitch, roughly 1,000-foot Grade III route up the center of Roan Wall, a big red slab split by a prominent corner system, on very high-quality granite with patina edges, friction slab, and cracks higher up.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the route itself, using the new double-ring stainless-steel bolted anchors present at each belay station; bring double ropes.
current.detailed_rack: About 14 quickdraws plus a single set of nuts and cams to 2 inches; all belays have new double-ring stainless steel bolted anchors.
current.pro_needs: Predominantly bolt-protected slab and face climbing with some natural gear on crack sections; a single light rack to 2" plus ~14 draws covers it.
bivy: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County

name: Roan Wall - Stage Right
beta: Shares its approach and lower access with Center Stage; before reaching Center Stage's start, traverse about 200 feet right to a pale/white slab between two obvious left-facing corners. Features a pale slab approach pitch, face pitches with friction cruxes, corner climbing, sustained slab sections with crimpy holds, and finishes on a unique pitch combining an overlap crack with low-angle face climbing. Climbs the same very high-quality granite as the rest of Roan Wall.
overview: A 10-pitch, roughly 1,400-foot Grade III route up the rightward slab of Roan Wall, offering stacked pitches of quality face climbing with friction cruxes, corner work, and a unique finishing pitch with an overlap crack and low-angle face climbing.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
current.descent: From the top of Stage Right, find a narrow ledge and work left and slightly downward to reach the top of the Center Stage route. From there, rappel Center Stage's bolted double-ring anchors (the face is described as clean and open) using double ropes.
current.detailed_rack: 10-12 quickdraws and a light rack of cams (small sizes up to 3 inches); double 60m ropes.
current.pro_needs: Predominantly bolt-protected slab/face climbing supplemented by a light cam rack on the corner and crack sections; double ropes needed for the Center Stage rappel descent.
bivy: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County

name: Southeast Ridge
beta: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead, follow the maintained Robinson Creek Trail north, cross Beauty Creek, and turn uphill onto the unmarked, unmaintained Beauty Creek Trail. Climb the brushy, steep Beauty Creek valley, cross a tributary around 5,200-5,260 ft, then ascend open meadow/scree to a small tarn at roughly 6,750-6,800 ft in a rocky basin. From the tarn, climb the loose scree slope (snow-covered in early season) north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge, then turn left (north-west) and follow the ridge about a mile over several false summits — mostly class 2 walking with a few class 3 sections and a narrow, exposed crux just below the true summit.
overview: The standard and easiest line on Robinson Mountain: a long trail approach up Robinson Creek and unmaintained Beauty Creek Trail to a tarn basin, then a scree climb to a gap on the southeast ridge followed by roughly a mile of class 2 ridge walking with a few class 3 sections — including a short, exposed knife-edge/gully crux — to the broad summit.

current.approach: From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 14-15 miles to the Mazama junction, then turn onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140) and drive about 7.5 paved miles and another 1.5 miles on gravel Forest Road 5400 to Robinson Creek Trailhead (elev. ~2,500-2,560 ft, with an information sign, picnic table, and vault toilet). From the trailhead, hike the Robinson Creek - Middle Fork Trail (#478) north for about 2.8 miles to the signed/bridged Beauty Creek junction (elev. ~3,560 ft) just past a bridge over Beauty Creek. Turn right (northeast/uphill) onto the unmarked, overgrown Beauty Creek Trail and follow it about 1.5 miles up the valley, staying northwest of the creek, to a tributary crossing around 5,200-5,260 ft, then continue up open slopes to the tarn basin at about 6,750-6,800 ft.
approach_variant_names: Robinson Creek #478 to the Beauty Creek trail #579, then the tarn basin
current.descent: From the summit, reverse the ridge scramble south-east along the crest back to the gap, downclimb the scree slope to the tarn basin, then follow the boot path/open slopes back down to the Beauty Creek tributary crossing (~5,200 ft) and down the steep, brushy Beauty Creek Trail to its junction with the Robinson Creek Trail. From there it is a straightforward 2.8-mile walk out the maintained Robinson Creek Trail to the trailhead. The loose scree section above and below the tarn is the main slow/careful-footing section on both ascent and descent.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard ascent — this is an unroped scramble.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection required; this is an unroped class 2-3 scramble on talus/scree and broken ridge crest.

name: Northeast Ridge (Nason Ridge Traverse)
beta: The finish of a longer cross-country ridge traverse rather than a stand-alone climb: from the Howard-Rock col, ascend Rock Mountain's northeast side (snow climbing and rock scrambling), then descend via the South Ridge-East Slope to the Rock Lake basin and exit on the standard Rock Mountain Trail. Requires solid off-trail navigation and, in early season, snow-travel skills (an ice axe was necessary on a June ascent).
overview: A cross-country mountaineering line up Rock Mountain's northeast side, reached by crossing the Howard-Rock col at the far end of a multi-summit Nason Ridge traverse (Mt. Mastiff - Mt. Howard - Rock Mountain), rather than via the maintained West Route trail.

current.approach: Begin at the Old Merritt Lake Trailhead off US-2 (~2,950 ft). Climb via Mahar Creek Ridge to Merritt Lake, then continue over Mt. Mastiff's Southeast Ridge and Mt. Howard's Northeast Ridge (both reported as snow climbs/rock scrambles) before dropping to the Howard-Rock col and climbing Rock Mountain's northeast side.
current.descent: From the summit, descend the South Ridge and East Slope toward Rock Lake, picking up the maintained Rock Mountain Trail in the Rock Lake basin and following it down the switchbacks to the Rock Mountain Trailhead on US-2 (a different trailhead than the Old Merritt Lake start, so a car shuttle or hitch on US-2 is typically needed).

name: Roofer Madness
beta: Pitch 1 (5.11+, ~25 ft) is a very thin traversing pitch where precise footwork is essential — a fall risks hitting the ledge below. Pitch 2 (5.10+) heads straight up the slab to the arete and tops out on Martha's Place. Fully bolted with 13 bolts total; the belay is split at a ledge partway up to prevent rope drag. Noted for excellent bolt placement.
overview: A short, bolt-protected 2-pitch 5.11+ sport testpiece on the downhill side of the Martha's Place bivy boulder in Waterfall Basin, finishing atop the boulder.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
current.descent: A short route typically descended by rappel or lowering directly off the bolted anchor system; the mid-route ledge anchor allows a controlled two-stage descent if needed.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted sport route; a set of quickdraws (enough for 13 bolts) is sufficient, no trad rack needed.
current.pro_needs: Bolt-protected throughout (13 bolts); no gear placements required.

name: Route C
beta: A well-bolted, slightly steep climb on jug holds. Climbers can follow the bolt line straight to the chains, or after clipping the 5th bolt, traverse right onto a solid horn and back left for a mellower ledge variation.
overview: A fully bolted one-pitch 5.9 sport route on jugs, the second bolt line after the obvious prow at Ice Box (Left Side); the easiest of the three routes at this crag.

current.approach: Spire Gully right (Alpenkuhl), part of the Hairpin Crags, is reached from the same large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 near Washington Pass used for Kangaroo Temple. Looking up toward South Early Winter Spire from the pullout, Spire Gully is the obvious gully just below and left; Alpenkuhl is its sunnier, south-facing right side (the left side is known as Tiger Wall). The approach is one of the shortest at Washington Pass — a direct walk/scramble of roughly 10-15 minutes straight up from the highway, snow-covered in early season and a worn boot path later in summer.
current.descent: Lower on a single strand from the fixed chain anchor at the top of the route, or rappel with a 60m rope; no walk-off is required.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted with 8 bolts to chain anchors — carry roughly 8-9 quickdraws and a 60m rope; no traditional gear rack needed.
current.pro_needs: Sport-bolted line; no trad gear required beyond quickdraws.

name: Northwest Ridge Route
beta: Park at a turnout across from a large boulder field on the northwest side of the mountain. Climb steeply up the hillside left (east) of the boulder field to gain the northwest ridge, follow it over Point 6315', transition onto the west ridge around 5,400 ft, and finish with a scramble up the summit ridge. In snow season, cliff bands along the ridge are typically turned via snow ramps.
overview: A steep, direct hike/scramble straight up Ruby's northwest ridge from a Highway 20 turnout — the most popular way up during winter and spring, when SR 20 is gated for the season.

current.approach: From Newhalem, drive or walk SR 20 east about 12 miles (0.4 mi west of Horsetail Creek, ~2.8 mi northeast of Colonial Creek Campground) to a turnout at about 1,900 ft elevation, directly across from a large boulder field on Ruby's northwest side.
current.descent: Retrace the ascent ridge, using snow ramps to negotiate cliff bands in winter/spring conditions; remove snowshoes for one cliffy section around 4,000 ft as needed on the way down as well.

name: Ruth-Icy Traverse
beta: Approach via the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail to Hannegan Pass, then follow an unmaintained climbers' trail south onto the Ruth Glacier and up easy snow to Ruth Mountain's summit. From Ruth, descend about 1,600 ft in two roughly 800-ft steps to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy, cross talus and glacier to a notch west of Icy's Northwest Spire near 6,500 ft, then climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd-3rd class terrain and a short 4th class summit gully to Icy Peak. The whole traverse is reversed to descend.
overview: A remote, two-summit alpine traverse linking Ruth Mountain's glaciated dome with the rugged 4th-class summit block of neighboring Icy Peak, connected by a high ridge/saddle traverse below the dramatic Nooksack Cirque. Widely regarded as one of the best moderate outings and finest viewpoints in the Mt. Baker Wilderness / North Cascades National Park backcountry, though it is considerably more remote and route-finding-dependent than the standard Ruth Mountain South Slopes climb.

current.approach: Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the South Slopes/Ruth Glacier route: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FR-32) up the Ruth Creek valley to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft, ~4 miles, ~2,000 ft gain), then the climbers' path east and south past the pond below the pass (faint, easy to lose), around a cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit (~6,600 ft) — see the South Slopes route for full trailhead-to-glacier detail, including the documented crevasse-fall hazard on the lower glacier despite its mellow appearance. From camp, the traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another ~800 ft (about 1,600 ft total off Ruth's summit) to the low saddle/col between Ruth and Icy at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft. Parties choose between a steeper, more direct 'death gully' line or supposedly-cairned heather slopes and game trails to climber's left holding 2nd-3rd class ground — the heather-slope option is the safer, recommended line. From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and talus/boot-path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then ascend talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper, aiming for a notch/saddle just west of Icy's Northwest Spire (~6,500 ft). From that notch it's another ~500 ft of 2nd-3rd class scrambling up an obvious left-hand, light-colored gully system to the base of Icy's summit block, where a 100-ft, 4th-class gully (solid jugs and ledges but real exposure) leads to the top. Helmets are standard here given loose rock and traffic funneled through a single gully. Note the true (highest) summit is the SE point, about 11 ft higher than the peak most maps label as the top.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass and Ruth Mountain first, then down to the Ruth-Icy saddle and across to the Icy Glacier
current.descent: From Icy's summit block, most parties rappel the crux 4th-class gully rather than downclimb it: there is a solid boulder/horn at the top used as a natural anchor, usually found slung with rap slings — there are no bolts on this route.
