Trip reports split between a single ~30m rappel that covers just the hardest, most exposed section (with easy 2nd/3rd-class downclimbing below) and a single full-length rappel with a 60m rope that gets the whole gully done in one shot. Plan on 1 rappel total; bring at least a 30m single or 60m rope so you have the option to skip the downclimb entirely. There is no other technical rappelling on the route. Below the gully, reverse the 2nd-3rd class terrain and talus back down to the Icy Glacier notch, cross back to the Ruth-Icy saddle, and climb back up and over Ruth's south/west slopes (re-gaining roughly the 1,600 ft descended earlier) to the notch/camp area northwest of Ruth's summit — there's no way to avoid this re-ascent on the standard car-to-car traverse. From there, reverse the South Slopes/Ruth Glacier descent: down the glacier's moderate but crevassed north slope, along the climbers' path past the pond below Hannegan Pass, and out Trail #674 down the Ruth Creek valley to the trailhead. Total round trip is roughly 16 miles with on the order of 8,000 cumulative ft of gain including the up-and-over of Ruth on the return; trip reports cite around 12 hours of moving time from camp, so most parties treat this as a long single push from a Ruth-area camp rather than a car-to-car day.
current.detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit plus a minimal alpine rack: one to two snow pickets per rope team for crevasse-rescue anchors, a few slings and locking carabiners, and (optionally) a thin rack of small-to-mid cams/nuts for the short rock step in Icy Peak's summit gully. Most competent parties move together on the glacier and solo or simul-climb the 3rd-4th class terrain in good conditions.
rack: 2-3 snow pickets and crevasse-rescue kit for the Ruth Glacier crossing
Harness plus slings/rap rings or tat for an optional rappel of Icy's summit gully (~100ft)
current.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal and glacier-oriented — pickets for crevasse rescue and occasional running pro — rather than a technical rock rack; the summit gully on Icy is typically soloed or simul-climbed rather than pitched out.
bivy: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
current.rope_note: Grade II glacier route: roped glacier travel required crossing the Ruth Glacier (mandatory ice axe, strongly recommended rope especially after early July); parties commonly carry 30m ropes. Final approach to Icy Peak's summit is ~500ft of 2nd-3rd class, then a 100ft 4th-class summit gully typically climbed unroped/scrambled.

name: Quien Sabe Glacier
beta: Boston Basin approach is steeper and rougher than Cascade Pass route. Trail is eroded and steep. Boston Basin sees less traffic and wider crevasse field on Quien Sabe Glacier compared to Sahale Glacier. Ascend left (north) side of Quien Sabe Glacier, watching for crevasses and selecting reasonable line—usually near center in steeper sections. Route between Sahale and Boston Peak summits (Sharkfin Tower is visible reference). Traverse south via col below the two peaks to reach Boston-Sahale Col. From col, traverse exposed snow to reach loose Class 3 summit scramble with persistent cornice into early summer. Final scramble is brief and loose.
overview: The Quien Sabe Glacier is the direct line up Sahale's north side from Boston Basin, climbing beneath Sharkfin Tower to the col between Sahale and Boston Peak before a short technical finish to the same 8,680 ft summit reached by the Sahale Arm route. It's more committing and more remote than the Sahale Arm approach and is usually done as an overnight from a Boston Basin camp.

current.approach: The Boston Basin approach starts at an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road roughly 21.5-23 miles from Marblemount (about 3,200-3,300 ft) - there's no formal trailhead sign, so watch your odometer. From the pullout, follow an old mining road/track for about a mile with minimal elevation gain, crossing Boston Creek. Watch closely for the unmaintained climbers' trail breaking off sharply to the right (cairns/flagging mark it, but it's easy to walk past); it climbs steeply through forest and a brushy old avalanche-slide path with sections of deadfall and loose footing. The path gains roughly 2,500 ft over about 2.5-3 miles to reach treeline and the lower Boston Basin camp (~5,300-5,400 ft), continuing to established upper camps around 6,200 ft. Plan on 3-4 hours trailhead to camp. Because this is a genuine climbers' path rather than a maintained trail, route-finding through the lower forest and slide-alder sections is the main approach hazard, and it can be greasy and slick when wet. Water is available from Boston Creek and seasonal snowmelt through mid-summer near camp. From high camp, rope up around 6,700 ft and make a rising traverse near the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower, picking a line up the Quien Sabe Glacier while avoiding crevasses - two common ascent lines (a left-side line and a more direct one) merge partway up. Expect to navigate a bergschrund via snow bridges around 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides in late season, before climbing to the Boston-Sahale col. From the col, a short but exposed snow traverse (crampons and axe recommended even late season) leads to the base of the summit block, finished with class 3-4 scrambling to the true summit.
approach_variant_names: Boston Basin climbers' trail and Quien Sabe Glacier
current.descent: Most parties reverse the col traverse and Quien Sabe Glacier back down to Boston Basin camp, staying roped through the crevassed midsection and re-negotiating the two snow-bridge crossings near 8,100 ft and 7,600 ft. Coming off the true summit block itself typically involves one short rappel rather than a downclimb - commonly to the southeast/south off the summit block on tat/slings at a natural anchor, dropping onto easier class 3 terrain; a single 30m rope is generally sufficient for this short rappel, though confident parties without rope sometimes downclimb the class 3-4 moves in reverse instead. Some parties skip reversing the technical col/glacier terrain and instead continue down the south side into the Sahale Glacier basin (as on the standard Sahale Arm route), which involves a second, longer rappel - two 30m ropes, or a single 60m rope doubled, off tat anchors on the south face - down to a ledge, followed by a short 3rd-class downscramble to the Sahale Glacier, then a hike out via the Sahale Arm/Cascade Pass Trail. Either way, expect real crevasse hazard on the glacier descent that increases through the season, plus loose, chossy rock on the south-side downscramble option.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier travel kit; a few pieces and slings for the summit block
current.pro_needs: Crevasse rescue gear; minimal rock pro for the summit

name: Sahale Arm / Sahale Glacier
beta: Begin at Cascade Pass trailhead off Cascade River Road. The first 2.5 miles feature 35 gradual switchbacks gaining 1,500 ft. Transition from forest to alpine meadows. Sahale Glacier is small and not very active. Route weaves SW to N side of summit block. The short chimney feature (5.0) on pyramid's south side serves as main crux with exposure. Few pieces of rock pro useful for final moves. Most groups don't rope for scramble but protection is reasonable. Descend via rappel (or 5-rappel sequence for full descent) and traverse SE to loose rocks, then steep snow downclimb (40-45 degrees) or face-in descent, followed by scree traverse and plunge-stepping down gentle snowfield to camp.
overview: Sahale Mountain (8,680 ft) sits at the head of Cascade Pass in North Cascades National Park, and the Sahale Arm route is widely regarded as one of the most scenic moderate glacier climbs in the Cascades — a hike-heavy approach through wildflower meadows on the Sahale Arm leading to a short, low-angle glacier and a final rocky summit block. It's also the standard northern jumping-off point for the multi-day Ptarmigan Traverse.

current.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the Cascade Pass Trail through old-growth timber via roughly 35 well-graded switchbacks, gaining about 1,800 ft in the first 2 miles before the grade eases through subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at about 3.5-3.7 miles. At the pass, take the left (north) fork signed for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open, increasingly rocky ridge crest - the Sahale Arm Trail, about 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft of additional gain, with views down to Doubtful Lake (a worthwhile ~1-mile, 1,000-ft side trip on a signed spur if you want water or to scout the basin) and across to Johannesburg Mountain, Magic Mountain, and Mixup Peak. The maintained trail ends around 7,200-7,600 ft at Sahale Glacier Camp, a cluster of rock-walled tent pads that also serves as the NPS-permitted high camp (wilderness permit required, quota-limited in summer). Total trailhead-to-camp distance is about 6 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain, typically 4-5 hours. Above camp, rope up for glacier travel - the Sahale Glacier is small and generally low crevasse hazard compared to nearby glaciers but should not be crossed unroped without current beta, especially late season - and ascend directly to the southwest base of the summit pyramid. From there a short, exposed stretch of steep snow and 3rd-4th class rock leads to a ledge just below the true summit, finished by a short, awkward chimney-like move (about 5.0) onto the summit block. Water is reliably found at Doubtful Lake and from snowmelt/tarns near Sahale Glacier Camp early-to-mid season, but sources can dry up by late summer, so carry enough for the switchback climb to the pass.
approach_variant_names: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
Car-to-car day push
current.descent: Below Sahale Glacier Camp, descent is simply a reverse of the Sahale Arm and Cascade Pass trails back to the trailhead. Getting off the summit block itself is usually done by rappel, though some parties downclimb it instead, often with a belay through the crux. Parties commonly rappel the south side, where the rock strata slopes away from the face and is comparatively free of loose blocks, off a well-used natural anchor - typically a cluster of several slings (often faded/sun-worn and worth backing up) wrapped around a large boulder, sometimes with rap rings added. With a 60m rope doubled (about 30m of rope per strand), most parties reach easier ground or a second station in a single rappel; with a 30m single line or 50m doubled, expect an awkward down-scramble to bridge the remaining gap, and some parties instead break it into two shorter rappels. From the base of the rappel, a short 3rd-class scramble/downclimb regains the top of the Sahale Glacier, which is then recrossed roped back to camp. No unusual descent hazards beyond the rappel itself and standard glacier crevasse hazard, which increases as the season progresses and the glacier opens up.
current.detailed_rack: A glacier rope and a few slings for the summit block.
current.pro_needs: Protection is minimal, with standard glacier-travel anchors and a sling or two on the summit block. The route is about easy glacier travel and a short scramble rather than rock protection.

name: Salish
beta: Begins on the far right side of the main face; a few fourth-class moves lead to a starting ledge below the shield's roof. A quick boulder move leads to the obvious shield, which ends at a rap tree (~5 m). The route connects into the Traverse pitch. An old hex and Eiger USA biner were found stuck in the shield, suggesting an earlier unrecorded ascent; the route is credited to the Salish people who occupied this land long before rock climbing existed here.
overview: Salish climbs the far right side of Osprey Wall's main face: fourth-class moves lead to a starting ledge below an obvious rock "shield," and a quick boulder move gains the shield's top at a rap tree that also serves as the start of Traverse.

current.approach: From the pullout, a short (~5-minute) woods trail leads to a large boulder/scree field at the base of the slope. From there, ascend and angle left for about 15 minutes to reach a mossy ramp system that marks the start of the wall. The route up the ramp climbs the mossy slab's far-left side, diagonaling toward the top right where a fixed rappel anchor (inspect before trusting) allows descent; a full 60m rope skips the mossy slab entirely, landing back at the scree field. Best conditions are summer when the slab is dry. Osprey Wall is a small, lightly-documented crag, so treat these approach specifics as generally reliable but not pinpoint-precise until verified on site.
current.descent: A rap tree marks the top of the shield; a single 60 m rope reaches the starting ledge on rappel. From the top, climbers can either rappel back down or continue across the ledge system via the Traverse pitch toward Prey's P1 belay.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack; the crack system "eats stoppers," so bring extra small-to-mid nuts.
current.pro_needs: Single rack of nuts/stoppers; extra small-to-mid sizes recommended since placements consume gear.

name: South Slopes via Emerald-Saska Col
beta: From a high camp in the basin between Saska and the Fern Lake/Pyramid Mountain trail system, climbers cross talus, scree, or lingering snow slopes to gain the south ridge/col between Emerald and Saska peaks. From there a short but exposed class 3 scramble along a narrow, sometimes knife-edged ridge crest leads to the summit. Parties describe an obvious scree/rock gully on the right (west) side of the ridge, followed by a rising traverse (cairned) on the right side of the ridge, then final class 3 scrambling to the top. It is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska/Emerald/Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
overview: Saska Peak is the third-highest peak in the Chelan Mountains and rises just northwest of its taller neighbor Emerald Peak (8,422 ft), 0.66 mi away across a connecting col. It's almost always climbed in combination with Emerald via that col, and strong parties often add Cardinal Peak (1.5 mi southeast) for a three-summit outing sometimes called the Entiat Bulgers. The peak sits deep in the North Fork Entiat River drainage inside Glacier Peak Wilderness — a long, quiet approach through fire-damaged forest rewards climbers with a genuinely remote basin and, in October, larch color on the descent.

current.approach: Standard access is the North Fork Entiat River Trail (#1437) from the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (el. ~3,940 ft, at the end of Forest Road 5606, about 35.3 mi from the town of Entiat via Entiat River Road/Forest Road 51 then FR 5606). The trail crosses old fire-damaged forest with blowdown for its first miles, enters Glacier Peak Wilderness at about mile 4 (free self-issue wilderness permit, filled out at the trailhead kiosk), and reaches the Pyramid Creek/Fern Lake trail junction roughly 7-9 miles in depending on trip reports and current trailhead access (road washouts have periodically forced parties to start several miles below the official trailhead — check current Forest Service alerts). From the junction, the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail climbs west about 1,000 ft over roughly 1-1.5 miles into the high basin between Emerald and Saska; most parties camp either at Fox Camp near the junction or push on to a larch-meadow camp directly beneath the Emerald-Saska col for a shorter summit day. In early September the basin below the col has a camp with running water and dense larches; scree on the way down is fast to boot-ski.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
Lake Chelan: Lucerne and Emerald Park to Milham Pass
current.descent: Descend the same col traverse and basin scree. In early-to-mid season, continuous snow below the col allows a glissade or boot-ski descent; by August-September this becomes loose scree and dirt requiring slow, controlled steps rather than good scree-skiing. Stay well clear of the cliff bands below the southwest face when snow-covered or icy — a documented February 2020 winter-ascent party lost a ski over these cliffs after misjudging the descent line in icy conditions.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection is placed; this is an unroped scramble for competent parties.
bivy: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble via broad gully to South Ridge; airy, exposed summit block with high rockfall danger and loose holds. No rope standard, though cautious parties may want a handline for the final exposed section.

name: SE Ridge AKA Shield Wall
beta: The Shield Wall is a prominent buttress visible from the Forest Service road below. The lower seven pitches climb generally modest fifth-class rock up the wall face, with a bolted first-pitch belay and two fixed bolts mid-pitch; the crux is a well-protected finger crack passing the second tower on the right. Above the wall, three 30m rappels alternate with about six more pitches (3rd class to 5.7) through the ridge's rock parapets and gendarmes to the summit. Expect to place only 1-5 pieces of protection on many pitches, with few opportunities to sling horns or blocks despite what older published descriptions suggest, and generally poor rock quality throughout.
overview: A serious Grade III alpine rock route up Mount Washington's southeast ridge: 5th-class climbing up the 'Shield Wall' proper, followed by exposed, loose parapets along the upper SE ridge to the true summit. Rock quality is generally poor to fair, protection is sparse in places, and retreat from partway up the route is reported to be difficult — a route for experienced alpine rock parties comfortable with runout, low-quality rock.

current.approach: From the road-end parking on Forest Road 2419 (off North Lake Cushman Road/FR-24), shared with the standard route, walk the old roadbed past the standard route's trail entrance to just beyond the Big Creek crossing (~3,100 ft); a way trail leads to the base of the southeast ridge's rock section. Follow an old roadbed across Big Creek and a climbers' trail up a rock rib, gaining roughly 1,600 ft to a bowl below the Shield Wall; a gully ascends up and left to a notch at the wall's left corner (~4,850 ft) where the technical climbing begins. In late May a steep snow slope sat between the basin and the first bolted pitch; the way trail up to that basin climbs roughly 1,600 ft and is easier to follow than the standard route's trail.
approach_variant_names: FR-2419 past the second Big Creek crossing, the way trail to the Shield Wall
current.descent: The route finishes on the summit ridge of Mount Washington, and the way down is the standard route rather than the SE Ridge, which would mean many rappels and the fifth-class cracks in reverse. Descend the Class 3-4 scramble to the basin; lingering snow often covers the upper slopes in early summer, and the narrow hourglass constriction can be bypassed on its west side. Below the basin, continue down through forest on the climbers' path to the FR-2419 trailhead at Big Creek, the same road end used for the approach.
current.detailed_rack: ["Single alpine rack: cams roughly #0.3-#3", "Set of stoppers/wires (~sizes 4-10)", "Alpine draws and extra shoulder slings (few horns/blocks to sling on this route)", "60m rope minimum recommended; some parties prefer a 40m lead line plus a separate 30m rappel line"]
current.pro_needs: Light alpine rock rack (small-to-mid cams, a set of wires, alpine draws/extra slings); protection is sparse on some pitches (as few as two usable placements reported on certain 60m pitches) and rock quality is generally poor, so careful gear placement and route-finding matter more than rack size.

name: Standard Route
beta: Sentinel is most often climbed, probably almost exclusively climbed, by parties doing the famed Ptarmigan traverse. From a high camp near the LeConte–Sentinel col or on the South Cascade Glacier, parties ascend a slope to a moat on the right side of a ledge/ramp that crosses the south face; the ramp is not difficult but demands care throughout, and the final section to the summit is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on snow and rock. A steeper variation exists via the west ridge, involving a steep snow ramp near 7,400 ft and a short low-5th-class rock step into a gully below the final ridge crest — this is harder than the standard line and should be treated as an alternate finish, not the default.
overview: Sentinel Peak (8,257 ft) is a remote summit deep in the Dome Peak / Ptarmigan Mountains section of the Glacier Peak Wilderness, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with its near-twin Old Guard Peak a few hundred yards away. It is not a stand-alone objective reached from a road-end trailhead — it's a side-trip peak bagged from a camp along the classic Ptarmigan Traverse, most commonly Yang Yang Lakes or the 7,300 ft Le Conte–Sentinel col. The South Cascade Glacier drapes its west slope and the Le Conte Glacier its northeast slope; views take in the Ptarmigan Traverse peaks from Formidable and Spider-Formidable Col south past Dome, Sinister, Gunsight and Spire.

current.approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road (paved/gravel Forest Road 15, inside North Cascades NP boundary — verify current road/washout status at nps.gov/noca before driving). Take the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain up open switchbacks and through Basin Creek/Doubtful Lake side-valley scenery to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), the last reliable trail tread and a good water stop. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country south on a boot path, climbing the Cache Glacier snowfield (permanent snow into late season; crampons and axe recommended) to Cache Col (~6,900 ft). The col's far (south) lip commonly corniced through mid-summer — this is a real hazard on both the ascent and the descent back over it. Drop steeply off the south side of Cache Col to the Kool-Aid Lake basin (established camps, reliable water). From Kool-Aid Lake, contour east around the toe of the Cache Glacier and climb to the 'Red Ledge,' a narrow, exposed rock ledge running beneath Art's Knoll that is the standard (least-technical) way through a cliff band and is considered one of the route-finding/exposure cruxes of the whole approach; in low-snow years the alternate Middle Cascade Glacier line can bypass it. Past Red Ledge, traverse to Yang Yang Lakes (~6,300 ft, good camping and water — most parties treat this or Kool-Aid Lake as their overnight base). From Yang Yang Lakes, ascend the broad Le Conte Glacier — a genuine crevassed glacier requiring roped travel — to the Le Conte-Sentinel Col (~7,300 ft), a flat notch atop the glacier with dry bivy sites and the jump-off point for the peak itself. From the col, easy scrambling leads onto snow filling the basin against Sentinel's west face; climb increasingly steep snow (can exceed 35-40°, crampons/axe useful) to its top, then follow an obvious ledge leftward (north) across the face past a short cliff band, then turn straight up steep, gravelly/scree terrain to a short step of upper-class-3/low-class-5 climbing, finishing with roughly 600 ft up the broad west ridge to the summit. Given the ~45 km round trip and glacier travel, this is realistically a multi-day trip (camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Yang Yang Lakes) rather than a car-to-car day climb for most parties.
approach_variant_names: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
Downey Creek and the south end of the traverse
current.descent: Descend the same line used on the ascent — the west ridge and the leftward-slanting face ledge — rather than the looser, steeper east ridge, which is explicitly warned against. Downclimb the short upper-class-3/low-class-5 step facing in, then descend the gravel/scree below it, pick up the diagonal ledge back rightward onto the west-face snowfield, and face-in downclimb or plunge-step the steep snow back down to the Le Conte-Sentinel Col. From there, reverse the approach: rope up again for the Le Conte Glacier's crevasses down to Yang Yang Lakes, back across the exposed Red Ledge, over Cache Col (cornice hazard on the descent to Kool-Aid Lake side just as on the ascent), and down the Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. No fixed or bolted rappel exists on Sentinel's standard route — it is a scramble walk-off/downclimb of the ascent line. Some parties place an optional single-rope hand-line or short rappel off a sling/picket to protect the low-5th-class step or the steepest snow near the col in early-season or wet conditions, but this is situational, not a required or documented feature of the route, so treat any rappel as optional protection rather than a mandatory technical descent.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit plus a light rock rack for Class 3-4 terrain
current.pro_needs: Glacier protection on approach; belay exposed steps
bivy: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers

name: Southwest Rib
beta: Ascend the obvious southwest buttress north of the SW Couloir. Route features diverse climbing from cracks to slabs with good pro on harder sections and some exposed runouts on easier terrain.
overview: The Southwest Rib is one of the most popular moderate multipitch alpine rock climbs at Washington Pass, climbing excellent granite on the west face of South Early Winter Spire with a famous dual-offwidth Bear Hug pitch and an airy slabby arete.

current.approach: From Blue Lake Trailhead (1 mile west of Washington Pass on Highway 20), hike Blue Lake Trail 1.25-1.5 miles to a clearing. At a small stream (possibly marked with cairns), leave the trail and ascend climber tracks through slabs parallel to the stream to reach the basin. Route base is identifiable by the distinctive Y-shaped larch tree. Total approach time: 1-1.5 hours; elevation gain to route base: 900-1,200 ft.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch
current.descent: Descend via the South Arete (the standard descent for the peak): downclimbing 3rd/4th class terrain to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted chain anchors back toward the Blue Lake basin. Expect delays at rappel stations on busy weekends since South Arete parties are often descending the same line.
current.detailed_rack: One 60m rope, a set of stoppers and cams to a #3 Camalot with doubles in the 1-2 inch range for comfort, plus one large cam (about a new #5) for the Bear Hug offwidth pitch.
current.pro_needs: Mostly good pro on the harder sections with a few runout slab stretches; bring one big piece for the Bear Hug.

name: Southeast Ridge
beta: Three short, low-fifth-class pitches follow the crest of the ridge from the notch at its base to the small summit, with huge exposure over the Boston Glacier for most of the climb. The rock is solid, high-quality granite and protection is generally good. It's a popular quick technical add-on to a Boston Basin trip (often combined with Sahale Peak or Boston Peak), but the glacier crossing and approach gully carry real objective hazard.
overview: Sharkfin Tower (8,120 ft) is a slender granite spire on the connecting ridge between Forbidden Peak and Boston Peak in North Cascades National Park, overlooking the Quien Sabe Glacier to the south and the Boston Glacier to the north. It's popular with Boston Basin parties as a shorter add-on to bigger objectives (Forbidden's West Ridge, Sahale, Torment). The Southeast Ridge is one of the range's classic moderate alpine rock routes: a short glacier crossing, a scree/snow gully, and three pitches of clean, exposed low-5th-class climbing on solid granite to a small summit with views into the Ptarmigan Traverse country. A harder two-pitch 5.10- line, the Southeast Face, climbs the wall just right of the ridge for parties wanting more challenge from the same approach.

current.approach: From the Boston Basin climbers' trailhead on Cascade River Road (~3,200–3,400 ft, ~21.7 mi from Marblemount; the upper road is prone to washouts, so check its status), pick up the unmaintained but well-worn Boston Basin climbers' path. It switchbacks steeply up through forest on old roadbed/boot path, crosses a couple of small streams (last reliable water before camp), and breaks out of the trees onto open meadow slabs. Expect roughly 3.2 mi and 2,500 ft of gain to the designated low camp (~5,300–5,700 ft), about 2.5–3 hours for a laden party; the high camp sits higher still on a meadow knoll around 6,300–6,400 ft and shaves real time off the summit day. From camp, contour/ascend slabs and easy snowfields on the left (climber's) side of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Sharkfin Col, rope up for glacier travel, and traverse east along the top of the glacier for several hundred feet until you're directly beneath the tower's obvious approach gully. This gully runs 35° snow in early season and degrades to loose class 2–3 scree/rubble by late summer; crampons and an axe (or trekking poles once it's melted out) help. Follow it up to a notch/terrace at the base of the southeast ridge proper. Route-finding here is the crux of the approach and has real consequences: a fatal 2005 accident on this peak began when a party climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully next to the standard line, so confirm you're in the correct gully (directly below the ridge, not an adjacent chute) before committing, and be alert for rockfall from parties above in this popular, loose corridor.
approach_variant_names: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — early season, snow gully
Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — late season, dry gully
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ridge: downclimb the upper class 4 crest a short distance (commonly cited as roughly 20 ft) to a chockstone/horn or fixed tat-and-ring station near the top of the gully, then rappel and downclimb the rest of the way back to the glacier along essentially the same line you climbed. Trip reports converge on roughly 4–5 rappels total to get from the ridge back down through the gully to the Quien Sabe Glacier — a short rappel or two off the upper ridge to regain the notch/gully, followed by two or three longer rappels down the couloir itself (some parties do the gully in two long raps of ~30 m each using two ropes tied together or doubled, others break it into shorter 15–20 m pitches on natural anchors). A single 60 m rope is generally enough for any individual station, and doubling/joining two ropes lets you skip stations in the gully if you're moving as a pair. Anchors are a mix of fixed tat-and-ring stations left by prior parties, slung chockstones and horns, and at least one station reported built from a couple of old pitons — quality is inconsistent and should not be trusted blindly. This matters here specifically: a well-documented 2005 accident on this exact descent involved a single-point natural anchor (one cordelette/webbing around a loose block, no backup) that failed under a multi-person rappel and resulted in three fatalities. Back up marginal anchors, rappel one at a time where anchors are questionable, and expect loose/blocky rock and, in shoulder season, wet rope and snow/ice in the gully. Once back on the Quien Sabe Glacier, downclimb/walk the snowfields back to camp, reversing the approach.
current.detailed_rack: Single set of nuts, cams to ~2 in (small-to-medium Camalot-size), 4-6 slings, cordelette or extra webbing for anchor building/backup, and a single 60m rope (double-rope rappels can speed up the descent through the couloir).
current.pro_needs: A light rack to about 2 in (nuts, small-to-medium cams) adequately protects the low-5th climbing; carry extra cordelette or webbing to replace or back up the sun-bleached tat commonly found at rappel stations.
bivy: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Descend exactly the way you went up (a bit of temporary flagging can help on the brushy class 3-4 terrain so you don't wander off-line), and do not reuse any old rappel webbing/tat found at the notch since it's likely to be years old — bring your own to replace it.
overview: A rarely-visited, multi-summited peak (North Peak, Middle Peak, and the 5,814' main/true summit) on the ridge roughly 3.6 miles southwest of the historic mining town of Monte Cristo, rising above Gothic Basin and the Weden Creek drainage in the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. Summit-register entries suggest it sees only about one party every four or five years, and the final terrain is steep, loose class 3-4 rock and brush rather than a simple walk-up scramble.

current.approach: From the Barlow Pass Trailhead (~2,360 ft, on the Mountain Loop Highway about 19.4-19.5 miles east of the Verlot Public Service Center / ~30.5 miles east of Granite Falls; Northwest Forest Pass required), walk south on the flat, gated Monte Cristo Road for roughly a mile, paralleling the Sauk River. The Weden Creek / Gothic Basin Trail #724 (an old miner's trail) splits off on the right just before the road's Sauk River crossing. Trail 724 climbs steadily from about 2,300 ft, fords Weden Creek (a real crossing that can be difficult during snowmelt or after rain), then switchbacks through forest and talus to roughly 5,000 ft over about 3.3 miles, passing beneath Foggy Lake/Gothic Basin around the 4.5-mile mark. Leave the maintained trail here and continue west on a flagged boot path past a first pond, then a second, smaller pool, re-crossing the Weden Creek outlet before traversing south — side-hilling steep talus and heather benches between about 4,800 and 5,200 ft — for just over a mile to Weden Pass (5,120 ft). Terrain is class 2-3 talus and heather until the final summit block, which turns into sustained class 3-4 rock and brush with one short step requiring a rope belay. Round trip is nearly 19 km (~12 miles) with substantial cumulative gain concentrated in the last few miles, so plan on a very long day (10-17 hours per available trip reports) or camp overnight in Gothic Basin. Key hazards: the Weden Creek ford, loose rock and brush on the class 3/4 sections, and exposed, sometimes-wet talus traverses between Weden Pass and the summit — a helmet is recommended.
approach_variant_names: Gothic Basin and Weden Pass
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: descend the northeast ridge back toward the notch/saddle below the true summit, then downclimb or rappel the short class 3/4 technical step just below the summit. Most parties rappel this step — a single 150 ft rope covers both the lead and the rappel, and the rappel itself is short, roughly 50-60 ft. This is a single rappel; no additional roped descents are reported lower on the route. Because Sheep Gap Mountain is an obscure, lightly-visited summit, no fixed bolted anchor is documented — expect to build or use a natural anchor (rock horn, chockstone, or sling around a block) rather than find bolts or chains, and bring gear/webbing to back it up or replace tat. From the base of the rappel, reverse the traverse back to Weden Pass, then retrace the talus/heather traverse and boot path down to Foggy Lake/Gothic Basin, and follow Weden Creek Trail #724 back down to Monte Cristo Road and Barlow Pass. Watch for loose rock on the class 3/4 terrain above and below the rappel and re-ford Weden Creek on the way out.
current.detailed_rack: No traditional rock rack is needed. A single 150 ft rope is what covers leading and then rappelling the one short (~50-60 ft) class 4 section - doubled through the tree anchor a 100 ft rope reaches only about 50 ft; that pitch can be protected with about three slings over horns or trees rather than cams or nuts.
rack: 30m rope (100-150ft sufficient) for the short roped pitch/rappel
1-2 long slings/webbing for tree rap anchor (bring your own, don't reuse old tat)
current.pro_needs: Minimal gear beyond a rope and a few slings for the short class 4 step; no cams or nuts are required.
current.rope_note: Mostly Class 3/4 rock and brush; one short pitch requires a rope belay going up, and the same section is rappelled off a tree anchor on descent. A 150 ft (45 m) rope covers both: 30 m is long enough to lead the short step but not to rappel it, since doubled through the tree anchor it reaches only about 49 ft.

name: Squak Glacier Route
beta: From a high camp near the Squak Glacier, rope up and climb glaciated terrain through a documented crevasse maze (~8,700 ft) to the saddle below the Roman Wall, then traverse south of Baker's true summit and front-point up steep, often icy slopes to Sherman Peak's summit ridge, which can be corniced with large rime-ice knobs. The final short section to the actual summit is typically climbed unroped.
overview: A glacier ascent of Sherman Peak via Mount Baker's Squak Glacier on the mountain's south side, approached from the same Schriebers Meadow trailhead as the Easton Glacier line but following a more easterly glacier path through a maze of crevasses to a bergschrund-guarded final summit slope.

current.approach: Approach from the Schriebers Meadow Trailhead (~3,366 ft) as for the Easton Glacier route, branching onto the Squak Glacier line rather than the Railroad Grade/Easton line; high camp is commonly established around 6,500 ft. In early June the Scott Paul trail is the usual way up to about 4,700 ft before joining the glacier line; camp at Crag View is near 6,100 ft.
current.descent: Reverse the ascent along the crater-rim ridge as far as practical, then make a shorter, safer downclimb (or ski descent off the north side, contouring around the bergschrund) back toward high camp rather than reversing directly over the bergschrund-guarded slopes.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier rope per rope team, pickets/ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors, and locking carabiners for rescue systems.
current.pro_needs: Standard crevasse-rescue protection (pickets/screws); no rock protection is placed. Steeper icy sections near the top may warrant a second tool for some parties.
bivy: Upper Squak benches, Sulphur moraine and the rock prow

name: Standard Route
beta: This is less a 'route up the peak' than the technical crux feature of Sherpa Peak: a free-standing granite pillar near the true summit. Parties typically combine it with the Class 3-4 ridge traverse to Sherpa's main summit. The crux move onto the pedestal has historically been done either by shoulder-standing a partner or by throwing/lassoing a rope over the pedestal's point; from there, bolt-protected friction slab gains the flat top, from which a single aging bolt is used to rappel back down.
overview: Sherpa Balanced Rock is a ~20-ft granite obelisk perched on the crest of Sherpa Peak (8,605-8,630 ft, figures vary), a satellite summit of Mt. Stuart in the Stuart Range, Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It sits about 100 yards from Sherpa's true western high point; a sight-level survey found the block only ~2 ft lower than that summit, so many climbers consider tagging the block the true top of the peak. Dave Mahre, with Gene and Bill Prater, made the first ascent in 1955. Reaching the flat top requires a short, bold, historically-protected sequence off an overhanging pedestal.

current.approach: Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it east/downstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with roughly 6,000 ft of climbing on the way in, and Longs Pass to regain on the way out; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.
approach_variant_names: Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and Table Rock
current.descent: From the top of the balanced rock, most parties do not reverse the shoulder-stand/friction sequence (considered the route's real crux to downclimb) and instead rappel a single fixed bolt/chain anchor at the summit straight back down to the belay ledge - a short (~20 ft) single-strand rappel that any rope length easily covers. From the ledge, downclimb or step off to the talus/blocks at the base of the pillar. From there, descent is a reversal of the approach: regain the ridge crest and drop back toward Table Rock and the Sherpa-Argonaut basin, picking down through the boulder field and the Class 2-3 gully system - loose, rockfall-prone terrain where a helmet is strongly advised, and where parties note the unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself, especially near dusk. Regain the climbers' boot path at the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction, re-ford Ingalls Creek, and climb back up and over Longs Pass to return to the trailhead. This is a single-pitch feature, so no multi-rappel sequence is needed for the balanced rock itself - the one bolted rappel off the top is the only roped descent on the Standard Route; parties climbing the broader Sherpa Peak West Ridge to reach the main summit (a separate, longer route) report needing several additional rappels off that ridge, but that is not part of this Standard Route's descent.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack and slings for the short summit sequence.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rack for the single 5.7 pitch — a few small-to-mid cams and nuts and extra slings to supplement the old fixed ring piton; the crux is the unprotected shoulder-stand entry more than the gear-protected friction moves above it.

name: East Ridge
beta: From a basin camp around 6,800 ft, follow the east ridge toward the summit; cairns and fixed slings/webbing along the ridge aid route-finding. The route passes around the balanced rock from the north side, which can involve a sketchy traverse over snow or wet rock in early season. The balanced-rock move itself is a shoulder-stand or rope-throw over a pedestal point to gain its east side, then bolt-protected friction climbing to the top, rated 5.7, with a rappel bolt atop.
overview: The East Ridge is the easier of Sherpa's two south-side ridge routes: broad blocky terrain and sandy benches at Class 3-4 with only brief low-5th-class steps, passing directly beneath the Sherpa Balanced Rock obelisk before finishing at the true summit. Because it's less sustained than the West Ridge, most parties descend via the West Ridge rather than reversing this line.

current.approach: Access is the same Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead used for the West Ridge: follow the Longs Pass Trail (#1229) over Longs Pass (~6,200 ft) and down to Ingalls Creek Trail, crossing Ingalls Creek and continuing on the climbers' boot path up into the Sherpa-Argonaut basin (see West Ridge approach for that shared section). From the basin, rather than aiming for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's-left (east), traversing a grassy slope and ascending a talus/scree gully to reach the prominent notch at roughly 8,000 ft, about 600 vertical feet below and east of the true summit. Gain the ridge crest about 100 ft above (east of) the notch via class 2 terrain. This line is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge approach, and picking the correct gully/notch is the main route-finding crux; a 50m rope is worth carrying from here since the route above uses fixed rappel slings at several obstacles.
approach_variant_names: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass, then east to the 8,000 ft notch
current.descent: Most parties do not reverse the East Ridge; the accepted descent is to finish near the summit, traverse to the top of the West Ridge, and go down using the West Ridge's established rappel line (two single-rope rappels past the crux, a short scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch - see the West Ridge descent for full detail) before dropping back to the basin and Ingalls Creek. Some parties do reverse the East Ridge directly, especially when combining the climb with the nearby Balanced Rock feature: this involves downclimbing/rappelling a vertical chimney using chained-together fixed rappel slings, then a rappel down a steep gully to an exposed slab, then another rappel after crossing the slab, finishing with class 3 downclimbing to the 8,000-ft notch. Expect roughly 2-4 short single-rope rappels off existing (sometimes weathered) fixed slings and chains rather than full ropelength raps; a 50m rope was reported as sufficient. Back up any suspect fixed anchors with your own gear. From the notch/basin, reverse the approach: descend to Ingalls Creek Trail, cross the creek, and climb back over Longs Pass to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams to 2 inches, a set of nuts, plenty of slings for horns, about 8 alpine draws, and a 60m rope for the steps and rappels.
current.pro_needs: The crest offers good crack and horn protection on steeper steps, with run-out moderate sections between. Carry enough slings to protect efficiently over the towers.
bivy: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
